# SupportJ60 — blind source review report (Round 60 attempt 3, wave 2)

VERDICT P01 SUPPORTED — "A mantle, whether stone or wood, was a very common spot to place an apotropaic mark, and, oftentimes, there would be quite a few over lapping marks." The quote appears verbatim in the body text ("Frequently small, faint, and hard to see, apotropaic marks are usually found where there is an opening through which evil could easily enter—doors, windows, and fireplaces."); the teaches (marks cluster at doors/windows/fireplaces as the openings through which evil could enter) and the entry claim (openings of the building) are both carried by that same sentence, with the fireplaces-as-weak-spot theme continued in the following sentences.
VERDICT P02 SUPPORTED — "The variety of this stone which resembles smaragdus in colour is often found with a white line running transversely through the middle" The page (Pliny's Natural History, book 37, Gutenberg pg62704) carries the quote verbatim ("(9.) Throughout all the East, it is the custom, it is said, to wear iaspis by way of amulet." — only a line-break whitespace difference); the teaches (Pliny reports the East-wide iaspis amulet custom) and the entry claim (Jasper/Pliny, it was the custom to wear iaspis as an amulet) are carried by that sentence.
VERDICT P03 NOT-SUPPORTED — Condition (1) fails: the page text reads "Other amulets do not cite the Gospels but use an apotropaic adjuration formula by which they banish evil spirits and diseases." while the packet quote says "evil whereas and diseases"; the string "whereas" occurs nowhere in the document (verified), so the quoted passage is not verbatim body text. The teaches and both entry claims ("evil spirits and diseases", "adjuration without scripture") are otherwise carried by that sentence.
VERDICT P04 SUPPORTED — "Over the nineteenth century, some other famous monks produced amulets which are now highly valued, and the acquisition of these amulets became popular among the high elite." The quote is verbatim ("Also like yantra, an amulet is effective only if made by a monk or adept famous for supernatural power (like Somdet To)."); the teaches (same efficacy rule as yantra, famous monk/adept maker) and both entry claims (the maker's power; the famous maker) are carried by that sentence.
VERDICT P05 NOT-SUPPORTED — Conditions (2) and (3) fail: the page (Kelsey DiSKO record for the Chnoubis Amulet, object 1963.04.0008) carries the quoted sentence verbatim ("It represents the amulet’s protective nature, associated with both the Egyptian god Chnum and the Greek god Agathodaimon." — curly apostrophe aside), but it contains no material on Anglo-Saxon charms, written slips, or mysterious words/letters/symbols (searched: Anglo, charm, slip, recipe, Leechdom, mysterious, letters — all absent), so neither the teaches nor the entry claim ("in five of the printed Anglo-Saxon D charms the amulet consists of a writing of mysterious words, letters and other symbols") appears on the page.
VERDICT P06 SUPPORTED — "Ritual masters purchase the mass-produced amulets at the New Year in bundles of two or three hundred for two thousand to two thousand five hundred VND, while they would pay five thousand VND for a single woodblock-printed amulet." The quote is verbatim apart from acronym casing ("The ritual masters empower mass-produced amulets in their own temples and sell them to clients for from twenty thousand to fifty thousand VND." — page prints VND); the teaches (ritual masters empower/bless mass-produced amulets in their own temples and sell for 20–50k dong) and both entry claims (the ritual market; mass production) are carried by that sentence.
VERDICT P07 SUPPORTED — "This early printed amulet from Germany, meant as protection for a woman in childbirth, is adorned with woodcuts illustrating the Hebrew months of the year." The quote is verbatim ("The main panel, framed by images of the zodiac, features an inscription banishing the demon Lilith, who, according to folklore, was Adam’s first wife." — entity-encoded apostrophe aside); the teaches (banishing inscription set inside a frame of zodiac images, naming Lilith) and the entry claim (printed childbirth amulet frames its main panel with zodiac images around an inscription banishing Lilith) are carried by that sentence.
VERDICT P08 SUPPORTED — "In Egyptian mythology Horus’ eye was injured or stolen by the god Seth and then restored by Thoth." The live page returned HTTP 429 (bot wall); the listed Wayback capture carries the quote verbatim ("An amulet in this shape was thought to protect its wearer and to transfer the power of regeneration onto him or her."); the teaches (wedjat-eye amulet guarded its wearer and carried regenerative power) and the entry claim (wedjat-eye shape, healed eye of Horus, protection and transfer of regenerative power) are carried by that sentence plus the preceding "the wedjat eye represents the healed eye of the god Horus".
